newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico fires drug agents, new evidence in scandal.
newsitem.headline: Mexico fires drug agents, new evidence in scandal.

text.p: The Mexican government fired at least 36 anti-narcotics agents on Monday and warned of more dismissals to come as police uncovered new evidence in the widening drugs scandal.
"Right now 36 have been fired, but this is not the last list," Attorney General Jorge Madrazo told reporters.

"Naturally we have detected and removed all those who were in contact at the Institute with Gen. (Jesus) Gutierrez Rebollo," the head of Mexico's National Institute for Combatting Drugs who was fired last week and arrested on charges of working for Mexico's top drug baron, he added.
Madrazo's office also said it had found more evidence linking Gutierrez to Amado Carrillo Fuentes, head of the powerful Juarez drugs cartel.
It said a search of the apartment complex in a residential area of Mexico City where Gutierrez lived showed that Carrillo had also spent time there, though not in the same apartment.
In Gutierrez's apartment, it said, police found "different elements which will allow investigations to continue" but gave no details.

In a nearby apartment in the same complex, they found an AK-47 assault rifle, a small wooden barrel filled with tequila and engraved with the name Amado Carrillo Fuentes, a letter addressed to the drug baron, $10,000 in cash, encrypted cellphones and bugging equipment.
Authorities have accused Gutierrez of accepting the luxury apartment he lived in from Carrillo.
The lastest news about traffickers' links to top government officals came as no surprise to Mexicans who have reeled from scandal to scandal in recent days.

Allegations by the New York Times that two state governors were tied to drug lords dominated newspaper front pages just days after Gutierrez's arrest and following sensational stories alleging that former President Carlos Salinas and his family received money and favors from drug lords during his 1988-94 administration.
In each scandal, all of the accused denied strongly the charges against them, but analysts said most of the recent revelations had been circulating as gossip for a long time.

"What are we surprised about?" asked managing editor Raymundo Riva Palacio in a column in Reforma newspaper. After listing a long series of drug scandals going back more than a decade, he said the real problem was "the tolerance, complacency and collusion of the Mexican state with the drug traffickers."

U.S. drug officials say more than 70 percent of the cocaine entering their country comes through Mexico, which is also home to several of the world's most powerful drug cartels and is a major producer of marijuana and heroin.

Diplomats noted that the U.S. and Mexican governments had tried to keep Mexico's failings in the drug war out of the headlines. While the United States has long been happy to lecture Colombia, Peru or Panama publicly about their failings in the war on drugs, Mexico has always received a pat on the back.

U.S. Ambassador to Mexico James Jones has never lost a chance to extol the virtues of the Mexican government, laud its commitment to the war on drugs and sing the praises of top officials like Gutierrez and former Attorney-General Antonio Lozano, fired last December amid charges of evidence-rigging and bribery of witnesses.
Jones praised Mexico's antinarcotics effort again on Monday.
